passage:
Saturday
At Anand's birthday today his aunt asked me where I'm from. I said Pune. She laughed. "No, no, where are you really from?" So I said my parents are from Imphal, and she said, "Oh! Your Hindi is so good!" I've lived here since I was two. Then someone's cousin asked if I eat dogs, as a joke. Anand told him to shut up, which was nice. None of it was mean, exactly. Everyone smiled. But it's the fourth "really from" this month, and every time I feel like I'm standing outside a glass window, looking in at a party I'm supposed to be part of. I didn't eat much cake. I just want to be from here without explaining.
— Himani

qa.q: What city did Himani first say when asked where Himani was from?
qa.a: Pune.

qa.q: What does the glass window image tell you about how Himani feels?
qa.a: It shows Himani feels like an outsider, singled out and lonely even among smiling people at a party.

qa.q: How could a friend like Anand support Himani beyond telling the cousin to stop?
qa.a: Anand could check in with Himani privately afterwards and gently tell relatives that questions like "really from" make people feel like outsiders.

qa.q: Why might Anand's aunt see her question differently from Himani?
qa.a: The aunt may think she is showing friendly interest, not realising Himani hears the same question again and again.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager repeatedly asked where they are really from and praised for their Hindi, feeling like an outsider.

passage: Every morning Mahima crossed the river on the ferry from the hamlet to the kasba high school, her notebook wrapped in plastic. The teachers liked her. That was part of the trouble. Another girl asked if her father could read. Each time Mahima smiled and answered. Nobody seemed to notice how many times it was happening. On the ferry home, watching the brown water, she counted them: seven, just this month. None of them was cruel. Together, they made the school feel like a place she was only visiting.

passage: The fest was in two hours and the science stall still had no labels. Noor was cutting, Naveen was writing, and the hall was so loud they had to shout. Dear Jeevan,
Something's been going round my head all week. In chemistry lab on Monday, Professor Sethi said, when I came in two minutes late, "Your people always run on your own time, no?" A few people laughed. I laughed too, which I hate. I've been deciding since then whether to say something. Part of me thinks I'm making a mountain out of it; it was one line. Part of me knows it wasn't the first. If I speak to him, he might mark me as difficult. If I don't, I carry it. Honestly the carrying is heavy. I might ask to see him after class and just ask what he meant. Or I might not. What would you do?
Imran
